text: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a support; a selected long effort arm can help lift a load. A ramp is an inclined plane: a sloping surface for raising a load along a longer route. A wedge narrows to an edge and can separate material. A screw has a spiral thread and can hold parts or lift a load. A pulley guides a rope; a fixed pulley can change pulling direction, while a suitable moving-pulley arrangement can reduce effort. A wheel and axle turn together: turning a large knob or crank can turn its smaller shaft.

These are useful physical arrangements, not six kinds of motor. Their benefit depends on the arrangement. They do not create energy or guarantee less force in every configuration. Gear-force vocabulary, formulae for moments and numerical mechanical advantage are not this source task.

In fictional CommunityA a team must move a box of books onto a low platform. The same box can be lifted directly or drawn along a stable ramp. The declared ramp route takes longer travel but less pulling force for this selected arrangement. A cart rolls the boxes along a level path, reducing resistance compared with dragging that same load in this model. The vehicle wheels are not claimed to be the same lifting arrangement as the knob-and-shaft example.

The model gives the team enough route space and adult-selected safe equipment. It also declares a narrow route where the cart cannot pass; carrying smaller loads on another suitable route is an available alternative. Learners compare access, effort, space and assistance needs rather than say newer technology is always better.

In fictional CommunityB a rope over one fixed overhead pulley lets an adult pull down while raising the same water container. Compared with lifting directly, the direction of effort changes. This one fixed pulley does not by itself halve the ideal force. The model also supplies a suitable two-supporting-segment moving-pulley arrangement with lower effort but a longer pull.

People benefit differently depending on reach, grip, available space and maintenance. In this model a damaged rope is removed from use until a responsible adult repairs/replaces it. Learners explain the benefit and changed limitation; they do not operate a well, lift water, suspend loads or test damaged equipment.

This is an original comparative model, not measured local data. For the same short book-delivery route and load, the model supplies three options: dragging a box, a hand-pushed cart with wheels/axles, and a fuel-powered vehicle. The supplied fuel vehicle emits exhaust on this journey; the manual cart has no exhaust from burning fuel during use. Building either option uses materials; the model does not say the manual option has no environmental footprint.

The existing firm path can carry the cart while retaining nearby habitat. A proposed widened path removes declared animal cover and vegetation. A longer existing route avoids removing that stated habitat but needs more time. Learners assess this movement technology’s benefit and environmental costs under both route conditions, not label a machine universally green.

forceComparisonProtocol.kind: Authored investigation design, no invented experimental result
forceComparisonProtocol.materials: Adult-selected low-load tabletop ramp, toy lever with stable pivot, pulley education kit and force indicator with its instructions; no suspended/heavy loads or sharp wedges/working tools. A supplied-data version can be used but is labelled as a model, not a child observation.
controlledComparisons: Same load, same start/end height: direct slow lift vs a longer smooth ramp. Compare sustained effort in the stated direction; do not compare a horizontal pull with an unrelated heavier load.
Same load/height: direct slow lift vs selected lever arrangement with longer effort arm. Explain that rearranging effort/load/pivot can change the result; not all levers reduce effort.
Same load/height: direct slow lift vs one fixed pulley, then a suitable moving-pulley arrangement. Include fixed-pulley direction change as a countercase to all-machines-halve-force.
learnerPerformance: Predict, carry out the selected safe comparison or interpret explicitly supplied results, record the force relation and describe direction/distance differences.
Base conclusions on the actual setup/data. An unexpected result needs checking friction/arrangement/control, not replacing results with the textbook answer.
Independently compare more than one type of machine with without-machine movement; identify same-load/same-height controls and reject a mismatched-load comparison.
forceComparisonProtocol.limits: Qualitative or quantitative evidence is allowed. Keep actual observations and supplied model data distinct; no whole-topic practical award follows from the supplied table. No older formal-force/moments/energy-work vocabulary gate or learner-attainment claim.

independentSourceProtocols.D1.1: Using the two fictional communities, identify the simple-machine arrangement and compare effects on daily tasks, assistance, access and limitations. Independently reassess the narrow route/damaged rope change. A generic old-versus-new story is insufficient.
independentSourceProtocols.D1.2: Identify the machine in the cart movement case. Compare supplied journey emissions and route habitat effects and propose a cause-fitting choice with a remaining constraint. Reject the unsupported claim that no tailpipe means no environmental cost.
independentSourceProtocols.D1: Independently synthesize machine-linked social and environmental benefits/costs using both community cases and the environmental route model. Name the mechanism’s actual contribution and changed-condition limit; do not count child codes.
independentSourceProtocols.D2.3: Use actual original six-machine-resource.html with teaching labels hidden. Independently name all six arrangements, point to each working feature, and explain the distinction. Do not provide labels during the check; later re-teach and assess a different ordering/model. Captions are teaching support, not assessed answers.
independentSourceProtocols.D2.4: Use the six authored everyday-use cards and diagrams. Then hide the teaching labels/captions and independently explain one appropriate everyday function for EACH category, connecting the arrangement to its force, direction or movement benefit. Naming a tool alone is insufficient; whole later gear-force vocabulary is not awarded.
independentSourceProtocols.D2.5: Use the controlled comparison protocol above; require multiple actual arrangements and a with/without comparison for each, plus fixed-pulley countercase and mismatched-load guard.
independentSourceProtocols.D2: Construct own explanation/model connecting ways of moving and repositioning a selected object to useful machine arrangements and controlled with/without force comparison. Overall scope must be reviewed independently; six labels alone do not establish the overall.

sixUseStudySet.use: A selected crowbar arrangement moves a nail by turning about its support; the learner studies a drawing, not a working tool.
A ramp gives a longer sloping path for raising a load.
A tapered doorstop fits under and holds an ordinary door in the supplied example; no emergency-exit use is prescribed.
A fixed pulley lets a person pull down to raise a flag or selected load. This direction benefit does not by itself prove reduced force.
A large knob turns its connected smaller shaft, as in the selected doorknob arrangement.
A threaded fastener turns to join selected materials; a picture/model supplies the example, not child tool handling.

forceComparisonAssessmentResource.kind: Original illustrative model data, not observed classroom results. Every row uses the same load and start/end height. The values are input-force readings in the same arbitrary force units, measured along the stated direction during slow, steady movement. They compare required push/pull force, not time, distance, energy use or total work. Values describe selected arrangements, not universal constants.

table.arrangement: selected lever, effort farther from support than load
table.inputDirection: down at the effort end, over a greater distance

table.arrangement: selected moving pulley with two supporting rope segments
table.inputDirection: along the free rope over a greater distance; this model includes resistance

requiredIndependentComparisons: Compare EACH machine row with direct lift: less/equal/greater input force, plus a direction or distance difference. Comparing machines only with each other or comparing time/distance instead of force is insufficient.
Identify direction change without force reduction; use evidence to reject the claim that every pulley halves force.

Changed lever: the effort point is closer to the support than the load, and the supplied input force is15 in the same units for the same load/height. Explain why the first lever conclusion cannot be repeated.
Reject a comparison using a different heavier load, stating what must match.
forceComparisonAssessmentResource.boundary: A supplied-data comparison can account for the source comparison operation. It does not award whole Testing Push & Pull Designs mastery, which requires actual building, testing, recording, improving and re-testing.

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: English
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Characters, settings, and events
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Identify characters, settings, and major events in stories; become familiar with key stories, fairy tales, and traditional tales and retell them with key details in sequence
evidence: Name the main characters in a story
Describe where and when a story takes place
Retell a familiar story including beginning, middle, and end events
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: After reading a fairy tale or story together, can {{name}} retell it to you in order — saying who was in it, where it happened, and what the main events were?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: English
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Listening to Texts Read Aloud
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Listen to and discuss poems, stories, and non-fiction at a level beyond independent reading; confirm understanding of texts read aloud by asking and answering questions about key details
evidence: Answer questions about a story or non-fiction text read aloud by the teacher
Discuss events, characters, or ideas from chapter books read to the class
Ask for clarification when something in a read-aloud is not understood
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: After you read a story aloud to {{name}}, can they answer questions about what happened — like who the main character was, where the story took place, and what the problem was?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: English
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Reading between the lines
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Ask and answer questions about key details in literary and informational texts; make simple inferences based on what characters say and do
evidence: Answer 'who', 'what', 'where' questions about a text using evidence
Infer a character's feelings from their actions (e.g. 'She's sad because she's crying')
Make logical guesses about unstated information using text clues
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: While reading a story, can {{name}} answer questions like "Why did the character do that?" or "How do you think they felt?" — using clues from the text rather than just guessing?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: History
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: My family and where we're from
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Identify the people in their family, where family members were born and raised, and how they are related to each other
evidence: Name the people in their family and say how each is related to them (e.g. 'Nan is Mum's mum')
Draw or complete a simple family picture or tree with photos or drawings of family members
Share where they and one older family member were born or grew up, using a photo, map or story from home
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you who is in your family and how they're related — like 'Nan is Mum's mum' — and where someone in the family was born or grew up?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: History
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Childhood then and now
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Identify continuity and change between aspects of their daily lives and their parents' and grandparents' childhoods, such as school, play, toys, chores, food and technology
evidence: Interview a parent or grandparent with prepared questions about school, toys or chores when they were young
Sort pictures into 'same then and now' and 'changed' (e.g. playing ball games vs video games, walking vs being driven to school)
Explain one continuity and one change between their life and a grandparent's childhood, using information from the interview
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: After chatting with a grandparent about when they were young, can {{name}} tell you one thing that's the same today and one thing that's changed?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: History
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Technology changes how we live
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Describe how technological developments changed people's lives at home and the ways they worked, travelled and communicated
evidence: Compare how a household job was done in the past and today (e.g. washing clothes with a copper and washboard vs a washing machine) and describe the effect on people's lives
Order pictures of transport (horse and cart, steam train, car, plane) and explain how each changed travel
Explain how communication changed from letters and telegrams to telephones, email and video calls, using one source as evidence
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how washing clothes, travelling or keeping in touch with family has changed since their grandparents were young?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: History
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Evidence from the Past
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Understand that everything we know about the past comes from evidence that has survived — objects, buildings, pictures, documents and stories — and use clues in that evidence to work out how people lived
evidence: Explain that we know about the past from evidence that has survived, such as objects, photos, buildings, documents and stories
Use clues from an old object or photo to infer how it was used and who might have used it
Explain why we know less about times or people that left fewer surviving objects or records
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} sees an old object like a rotary phone or a washboard at a museum, can they use clues to work out how it was used — and explain that surviving objects like this are how we know about the past?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: History
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Vocabulary: historical thinking
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Know and use the vocabulary of historical thinking — source, evidence, primary source, secondary source, artefact, chronology, chronological order, BC/BCE, AD/CE, century, decade, era, period, timeline, excavation, archaeologist, interpretation, corroborate, bias, perspective — and apply these terms when discussing how we know about the past and how reliable our knowledge is
evidence: Correctly use BC/BCE and AD/CE to place events in time and explain what the letters stand for
Distinguish between a primary source and a secondary source with an example of each
Use 'evidence', 'interpretation', and 'bias' correctly in a sentence about a historical source
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: If you asked {{name}} whether something they read in a history book was definitely true, could they explain why it might not be — using words like 'source', 'evidence', or 'bias'?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: Science
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Reducing Human Impact
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air, and other living things in the local environment
evidence: Identify at least three ways humans negatively impact the local environment (litter, pollution, habitat destruction)
Propose at least three solutions to reduce human impact (recycling, reducing waste, conserving water, planting trees)
Explain how each solution helps protect land, water, air, or living things
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} suggest ways people can help the environment — like recycling, not littering, saving water, or planting trees?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: Science
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Pushes & Pulls
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Understand that pushes and pulls are forces that can change the speed or direction of an object's motion, and compare the effects of different strengths and directions
evidence: Describe a push and a pull as types of force that make objects move, speed up, slow down, or change direction
Compare the effects of a gentle push versus a strong push on the same object
Predict the direction an object will move based on the direction of the applied force
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that pushing a toy car harder makes it go faster, and pushing it sideways makes it change direction?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: Science
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Shape and material change movement
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Describe how objects move (roll, slide, bounce, spin) and how an object's own size, shape or material influences the way it moves
evidence: Roll a ball and a block down the same ramp and explain that the round shape rolls while the flat-sided block slides or stops
Drop a rubber ball and a play-dough ball and explain that the material makes one bounce and the other squash
Compare how a big and a small ball roll down a ramp and describe the difference they notice
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: When playing with balls and blocks, can {{name}} explain why the round ball rolls away but the block doesn't — and why a rubber ball bounces but a play-dough ball goes splat?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: Science
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Testing Push & Pull Designs
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Analyse data to determine if a design solution works as intended to change the speed or direction of an object with a push or pull
evidence: Test a simple design (e.g. ramp, launcher) and collect data on whether it meets the goal
Analyse results to determine if the design works as intended
Suggest modifications based on the data to improve the design's performance
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a ramp to make a ball go into a cup, can they test it and figure out what to change if the ball misses?

wholeClaimSnapshots.subject: Science
wholeClaimSnapshots.name: Observing with simple equipment
wholeClaimSnapshots.description: Observe closely using simple equipment such as hand lenses, and use observations to describe, compare, and identify things
evidence: Use a hand lens or other simple equipment to make detailed observations
Describe observations using specific vocabulary (colour, shape, size, texture, pattern)
Compare two objects based on careful observation, noting similarities and differences
wholeClaimSnapshots.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a magnifying glass to look carefully at something like a leaf or an insect and describe in detail what they see?
